topic: Law fact / myth-buster: an FIR over a social media post does not mean automatic arrest - intent needed under Section 353(2) BNS, no repeat FIRs for the same post, Section 35 BNSS and Arnesh Kumar apply (Sri Sandeep Kumar v. State of Karnataka, Crl. P. No. 13010 of 2026, 2026 LiveLaw (Kar) 425)

slides.title: FIR over a post? It does **not** mean arrest
slides.subtitle: Three common myths about police cases over **social media posts**, and what the Karnataka High Court has now said.
slides.cite: **Sri Sandeep Kumar v. State of Karnataka**, Crl. P. No. 13010 of 2026 · 2026 LiveLaw (Kar) 425 · Justice M. Nagaprasanna

slides.label: Myth 1
slides.title: "An FIR means **instant arrest**"
bullets: **Fact:** registering a case does not by itself justify an arrest, the High Court said.
Police must follow **Section 35 BNSS** and the Supreme Court's ruling in **Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar**.
An arrest must be **justified** under the law in each case. It cannot be made **mechanically** just because an FIR exists.

slides.label: Myth 2
slides.title: "Sharing news is **always** a crime"
bullets: Here, an X page admin had reposted a news report about a stalking incident. Police booked him under **Section 353(2) BNS**.
**Fact:** this offence needs an **intention** to create enmity between groups. Plain reporting or criticism is not enough.
The post named no group, so the court **quashed** the FIR.

slides.label: Myth 3
slides.title: "Every complaint means a **new FIR**"
bullets: Police had registered **seven FIRs** over the same incident. The court called this shocking.
**Fact:** if complaints are about the same post or incident, police must first check whether a case is **already registered**.
A fresh FIR should not be filed just because a **different person** complains.
slides.note: **Law fact:** police must also check that the complaint, read as it is, shows every ingredient of the offence, not just **copy the section**.

slides.label: Keep in mind
slides.title: This is **not** a free pass
bullets: Posts made with intent to spread hatred or create enmity between groups can still be a **crime**.
Check facts before you share, and think about **how** you word a post.
This post is for information only, not legal advice.

caption:
Posted something online and now there's an FIR? Here's what the law actually says 📱⚖️

Myth 1: "An FIR means instant arrest." No. The Karnataka High Court has said that registering a case does not by itself justify an arrest. Police must follow Section 35 of the BNSS and the Supreme Court's guidelines in Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar.

Myth 2: "Sharing a news report is always a crime." No. In this case, an X page admin was booked under Section 353(2) BNS for reposting a news report about a stalking incident. The court said this offence needs an intention to create enmity between groups. The post named no group, so the FIR was quashed.

Myth 3: "Every new complaint means a new FIR." No. Police had filed seven FIRs over one incident, which the court called shocking. Police must first check whether a case on the same post or incident is already registered. The court asked Karnataka's DG and IGP to make sure every police officer follows these guidelines.

Keep in mind: this is not a free pass. Posts meant to spread hatred between groups can still be a crime. Check facts before you share.

Case: Sri Sandeep Kumar v. State of Karnataka, Crl. P. No. 13010 of 2026, 2026 LiveLaw (Kar) 425
Bench: Justice M. Nagaprasanna, Karnataka High Court
